# Optimal regularity for minimizers of the prescribed mean curvature functional over isotopies

**Authors:** Lorenzo Sarnataro Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540, USA Email address: lorenzos@princeton.edu and Douglas Stryker Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540, USA Email address: dstryker@princeton.edu

## Abstract

We prove the optimal $C^{1,1}$ regularity for minimizers of the prescribed mean curvature functional over isotopy classes. As an application, we find an embedded sphere of prescribed mean curvature in the round 3-sphere for an open dense set of prescribing functions with $L^{\infty}$ norm at most 0.547.

### 1. Introduction

Given a Riemannian manifold $(M^{n},g)$ and a function $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ , a two-sided immersion $\Sigma^{n-1}\to M$ is said to have prescribed mean curvature $h$ if the mean curvature of the immersion satisfies $H_{\Sigma}=h|_{\Sigma}\cdot\nu_{\Sigma}$ , where $\nu_{\Sigma}$ is a continuous unit normal vector field along $\Sigma$ . The problem of the existence of prescribed mean curvature hypersurfaces has been a rich source of motivation for work in geometric analysis.

An essential observation is that $h$ -prescribed mean curvature hypersurfaces arise as critical points of the $h$ -prescribed mean curvature functional

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega):=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial\Omega)-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{n}, $$

where $\Omega\subset M$ is an open set with smooth boundary. As in the study of minimal hypersurfaces and the area functional, this observation enables the utilization of variational techniques to produce $h$ -prescribed mean curvature hypersurfaces.

The simplest variational technique to produce critical points of a functional is to minimize the functional over some nontrivial class. In ambient dimensions 3 through 7, classical work of [FF60], [Fle62], [DG65], [Alm66], [Sim68], and [HS79] guarantees that any minimizer of area in a Riemannian manifold over integral currents with a fixed boundary is a smooth embedded minimal hypersurface. In the same dimensions, these results have been adapted by [Mor03] (see [ZZ20, Theorem 2.2]) to the prescribed mean curvature setting, where the minimization of $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ occurs over Caccioppoli sets that are allowed to differ from a fixed initial Caccioppoli set in a sufficiently small region $U\subset M$ . In this setting, the boundary of any minimizer in $U$ is a smooth embedded $h$ -prescribed mean curvature hypersurface.

While this regularity theory is very powerful, it is important to remember that the classes over which the minimization occurs are very large. In particular, elements in the same class can have arbitrarily complicated topology. Hence, we cannot draw any general conclusions about the topology of minimizers, which would be a natural hope for any geometric problem.

In the case of the area functional (i.e. $h=0$ ) in 3-manifolds, there has been significant work studying the regularity of minimizers of area over smaller classes with controlled topology. A major breakthrough was the work of [AS79], where minimizers of the area functional in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ over embedded disks with certain fixed boundaries are shown to be smooth embedded minimal surfaces. By an ingenious procedure to simplify the topology of elements in a minimizing sequence, [MSY82] used the regularity of [AS79] to show that minimizers of the area functional in a closed 3-manifold over an isotopy class11 1 We emphasize that isotopies preserve the topology of any submanifold. are smooth embedded minimal surfaces.

Despite the successful application of the regularity theory of [AS79] and [MSY82] in producing minimal surfaces with controlled topology in 3-manifolds (see for example [Smi83], [CDL03], [DLP10], [HK19], [Ket22]), there has been no generalization22 2 A result along these lines is claimed in [Yau01]; see later in the introduction for a discussion of this paper. of these techniques to the functional $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ .

In this paper, we generalize of the ideas of [AS79] and [MSY82] to the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ functional. For an open set $U\subset M$ , we let $\mathcal{I}(U)$ denote the set of isotopies $\phi:[0,1]\times M\to M$ satisfying:

- • $\phi(t,\cdot):M\to M$ is a smooth diffeomorphism,

- • $\phi(0,\cdot)=\mathrm{id}$ ,

- • and $\phi(t,x)=x$ for $x\notin U$ .

Our goal is to deduce the regularity of minimizers for the problem

$$ \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\Omega_{0})). $$

We deduce the following regularity statement.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function, and let $c:=\sup_{M}|h|$ . Let $U\subset M$ be a sufficiently small (see §14 for a precise definition) open set with $C^{1}$ boundary, and let $\Omega_{0}\subset M$ be an open subset with smooth boundary having tranverse intersection with $\partial U$ . Let $\{\phi_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{I}(U)$ , $\Omega_{k}:=\phi_{k}(1,\Omega_{0})$ , and $\Sigma_{k}:=\partial\Omega_{k}\cap U$ be a sequence satisfying

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega_{k})\leq\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\Omega_{0}))+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ . Then there is a varifold $V$ , an open set $\Omega\subset U$ , and a subsequence (not relabeled) so that

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{k}\cap U}\xrightarrow{L^{1}}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{k}\cap U}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ \mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k})\rightharpoonup V. $$

$V$ is an integer rectifiable varifold with $c$ -bounded first variation. For every $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , we have $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)=n_{x}\in\mathbb{N}$ . If $h(x)\neq 0$ , then $n_{x}\in\{1\}\cup 2\mathbb{N}$ . For every $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , there is a neighborhood $W_{x}$ of $x$ so that the following hold.

- • $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\sum_{l=1}^{n_{x}}\mathbf{v}(N_{l},1)$ , where $N_{l}\subset W_{x}$ is a $C^{1,1}$ surface with $c$ -bounded first variation. Moreover, each $N_{l}$ is on one side of $N_{l^{\prime}}$ intersecting tangentially at $x$ for any $l,\ l^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,n_{x}\}$ .

- • If $n_{x}=1$ , then – $\|V\|\llcorner W_{x}=|D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega}|\llcorner W_{x}$ , – $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,1)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}$ is a smooth stable surface with prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to the set $\Omega\cap W_{x}$ .

- • If $h(x)\neq 0$ and $n_{y}=2n$ for all $y\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|\cap W_{x}^{\prime}$ for an open set $W_{x}^{\prime}\subset W_{x}$ containing $x$ , then $V\llcorner G(W^{\prime}_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,2n)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}^{\prime}$ is a smooth stable minimal surface. Moreover, $\Omega\cap W_{x}^{\prime}=W_{x}^{\prime}\setminus N$ if $h(x)>0$ , and $\Omega\cap W_{x}^{\prime}=\varnothing$ if $h(x)<0$ .

- • If $h(x)\neq 0$ , $n_{x}=2n$ , and there is a sequence $x_{j}\to x$ with $x_{j}\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ and $n_{x_{j}}\neq 2n$ , then $n=1$ and the surfaces $N_{1},\ N_{2}\subset W_{x}$ additionally satisfy that the generalized mean curvature of $N_{1}$ points towards $N_{2}$ and vice versa. Moreover, the set $\Gamma=\partial(N_{1}\cap N_{2})\cap W_{x}$ is locally contained in a $C^{1,\alpha}$ curve and satisfies $\mathcal{H}^{1}(\Gamma)<+\infty$ .

Suppose additionally that $U$ is a sufficiently small geodesic ball. Then there is a neighborhood $Y$ of $\partial U$ with $V\llcorner G(Y,2)=\mathbf{v}(N,1)$ , where $N\subset Y$ is a smooth stable surface of prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to $\Omega$ satisfying $\partial N=\partial\Sigma$ .

In §3, we provide the details of examples that show that this regularity is sharp. We note that an adaptation of [MSY82] to the constant mean curvature setting with a stronger regularity conclusion than Theorem 1.1 was claimed in [Yau01, Theorem 2.1], but without a detailed proof. It appears that the example in §3.2 supplies a counterexample to this statement. In any case, this example illustrates an essential obstruction to a proof along the lines of [AS79] and [MSY82].

#### Remark 1.2.

In groundbreaking work, [WZ23a] prove the existence of 4 embedded minimal spheres in a generic metric on $S^{3}$ , which solves an important and longstanding conjecture in the theory of minimal surfaces. The proof of [WZ23a] uses extensively Theorem 1.1 as well as the new ingredients of the proof we develop in this work.

#### 1.1. Application to existence in the 3-sphere

Before unpacking the ideas of our proof of Theorem 1.1, we present a modest application of the theory to the existence of embedded $h$ -prescribed mean curvature 2-spheres in some metrics on $S^{3}$ . Since any embedded 2-sphere in $S^{3}$ can be moved by isotopies to a constant map, minimization techniques fail to produce nontrivial examples. Hence, we require a min-max variational approach.

To motivate our result, we recall the following question of Yau.

#### Question 1.3 ([Yau82, Problem 59]).

For which smooth functions $h:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}$ does there exist an embedded sphere with prescribed mean curvature $h$ (with respect to the flat metric)?

For progress towards Question 1.3 (and related problems) relying more on PDE techniques, we refer to [BK74], [TW83], [Ger98], [Ye91], [PX09], and [EFPS24]. There is also partial progress outside the min-max framework in [Yau97]. For progress towards 1.3 without topological control, we refer to [Maz22].

Since noncompact ambient spaces present unique difficulties for min-max theory, we consider the analogous question in $S^{3}$ .

#### Question 1.4.

For which smooth functions $h:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}$ does there exist an embedded sphere with prescribed mean curvature $h$ (with respect to the round metric)?

For the area functional, a min-max variational framework was developed by [Alm65], [Pit81], and [SS81] to produce a closed embedded minimal hypersurface in any closed Riemannian manifold of dimension between 3 and 7. These techniques have been refined to produce an abundance of closed minimal hypersurfaces (see [MN17], [LMN18], [IMN18], [MNS19], and [Son23]). This approach was successfully adapted to the functional $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ in [ZZ19] and [ZZ20]. In these works, min-max is carried out over similarly large classes of hypersurfaces without controlled topology, and the regularity theory relies on the classical regularity theory for minimizers discussed earlier in the introduction. Hence, we cannot draw any general conclusions about the topology of the resulting minimal hypersurfaces.

An alternative min-max approach in the minimal hypersurfaces case was developed by Guaraco ([Gua18]) and Gaspar-Guaraco ([GG16], [GG19]) using phase transitions for the Allen-Cahn equation, building on the regularity theory of Hutchinson-Tonegawa [HT00], Tonegawa [Ton05] and Tonegawa-Wickramasekera [TW12]. (We refer the reader to [Dey22] for a comparison between the Almgren-Pitts theory and the Allen-Cahn theory.) Similarly, [BW20] developed an analogue of the Allen-Cahn min-max approach for prescribed mean curvature hypersurfaces, building on the regularity theory developed in [BW18] and [BW19]. We emphasize that [BW20] only applies to nonnegative prescribing functions. As above, the topology of the produced hypersurfaces from these techniques is uncontrolled.

A min-max approach for the area functional in closed 3-manifolds that controls the genus of the produced minimal surface, called Simon-Smith min-max, was developed by [Smi83] (see [CDL03] and [DLP10]), building on the regularity theory of [AS79] and [MSY82]. In particular, it follows from these works that every metric on $S^{3}$ admits an embedded minimal sphere. For progress towards the existence of more embedded minimal spheres using this approach, we refer the reader to [HK19].

As an application of our regularity theory, we develop a min-max approach for the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ functional along the lines of Simon-Smith. In particular, we give the following partial answer to Question 1.4.

#### Theorem 1.5.

There is an open dense set $\mathfrak{P}\subset\{h\in C^{\infty}(S^{3})\mid|h|\leq 0.547\}$ so that there is an embedded sphere with prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to the round metric for any $h\in\mathfrak{P}$ . In particular, $\{h\in C^{\infty}(S^{3})\mid 0<h\leq 0.547\}\subset\mathfrak{P}$ .

The restriction to an open dense set is the same restriction from [ZZ20]. We recall that unique continuation is an important ingredient in the regularity theory for min-max surfaces. It follows from [ZZ20, Proposition 3.8 and Corollary 3.18] that unique continuation holds for an open dense set of prescribing functions that includes all positive functions.

The restriction to functions with $L^{\infty}$ norm bounded by 0.547 is the more significant assumption. This restriction is a consequence of the more delicate regularity theory for minimizers of the functional (1.1) over isotopies, as compared to the cleaner regularity conclusion for the area functional. We emphasize that our regularity theory is sharp, so it is not clear how to extend the existence theory beyond this class of prescribing functions using the techniques developed in this paper. Moreover, we are not aware of any counterexamples for large prescribing functions in this setting, so the question remains open.

Outside the setting of the round metric on $S^{3}$ , it is natural to consider the following related problem.

#### Question 1.6.

For which metrics $g$ on $S^{3}$ and which constants $c\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ does there exist an embedded sphere with constant mean curvature $c$ (with respect to the metric $g$ )?33 3 As a point of reference, it is conjectured in the introduction of [RS20] that there is a positive answer to 1.6 for any $c$ and any metric $g$ with positive sectional curvature.

Outside the min-max framework, there has been considerable progress on the existence of constant mean curvature immersed spheres in homogeneous 3-manifolds (see [DM13], [Mee13], [MMPR21], and [MMPR22]).

A min-max approach using the Dirichlet energy was developed in [SU81] to produce branched immersed minimal spheres. This approach was adapted to the constant mean curvature setting by [CZ23], where they show that every metric on $S^{3}$ admits a branched immersed sphere of constant mean curvature $c$ for almost every $c\in\mathbb{R}$ . However, it is unclear if the branched immersions produced by these techniques are genuine immersions, let alone embeddings.

Using our regularity theory, we provide the following partial answer to (1.6).

#### Theorem 1.7.

There are explicit constants $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ and $c_{0}>0$ so that if $(S^{3},g)$ is the induced metric of a graph over the round 3-sphere $\mathbf{S}^{3}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with $C^{2}$ norm bounded by $\varepsilon_{0}$ 44 4 By this, we mean that $(S^{3},g)$ is the induced metric of $\{x+f(x)\mid x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}+x_{4}^{2}=1,\ x_{5},\ldots,x_{N}=0\}$ where $N\geq 4$ and $f:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}$ satisfies $\|f\|_{C^{2}}\leq\varepsilon_{0}$ . and $0\leq c\leq c_{0}$ , then $(S^{3},g)$ admits an embedded sphere with constant mean curvature $c$ .

We remark that a key feature of Theorems 1.5 and 1.7 is that the restrictions on the prescription function and metric are explicit. Indeed, we expect that versions of these theorems hold with inexplicit constants by an implicit function theorem argument, using only the well-established existence theory for minimal spheres. Unlike such a result, our work provides actual testable criteria for existence.

#### 1.2. Idea of the proof of regularity

The proof of 1.1 follows the same strategy as [AS79] and [MSY82]. For clarity, we outline the approach of [AS79] and [MSY82], and then highlight the key differences.

- (1) Reduce the problem of minimizing area in an isotopy class to the problem of minimizing area over disks. In [MSY82], a procedure called $\gamma$ -reduction is introduced. In essence, $\gamma$ -reduction is used to delete small necks that either generate nontrivial topology or separate large components. By applying the $\gamma$ -reduction procedure a maximal number of times to a minimizing sequence for area over isotopies (and checking that the limit surface does not change), [MSY82] use the $\gamma$ -irreducibility property to show that the new sequence is a minimizing sequence for area over disks in any small ball.

- (2) Reduce the problem of minimizing area over disks to the problem of minimizing area over “stacked disks” in a cylinder. By zooming in along a minimizing sequence for area over disks at a point where the limit has a tangent plane, [AS79] use area comparison estimates to throw away components that are not close to the tangent plane in a small ball, without changing the limit. Therefore, it suffices to study a minimizing sequence for area over disjoint unions of disks with homotopically nontrivial boundary in a fixed cylinder. We call disks in this arrangement “stacked disks”.

- (3) Reduce the problem of minimizing area over many stacked disks in a cylinder to the problem of minimizing area over one stacked disk in a cylinder. To isolate one disk from many in the stacked disks arrangement, [AS79] develop a simple procedure to disentangle intersecting disks without increasing area. It then suffices to study a minimizing sequence for area over stacked disks with only one disk.

- (4) Conclude by Allard’s regularity. For a minimizing sequence for area over stacked disks with one disk, it is easy to obtain good lower and upper bounds for area. These estimates allow [AS79] to deduce the smooth regularity of the limit using the regularity theorem of [All72].

Steps (1) and (2) work for $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ with only technical modifications. For example, we make frequent use of the following basic idea. In the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ case, inequalities will have an extra volume term as compared to the area functional case. We absorb the volume term into the area terms using the isoperimetric inequality. The resulting inequalities resemble the analogous inequalities in the case of the area functional, only with slightly worse coefficients.

The essential difficulty is adapting steps (3) and (4). To highlight the key difference from the area functional, consider the case illustrated in Figure 1. In this case, we have a stack of two disks in a cylinder which is the boundary of the disjoint union of the set above the top disk and the set below the bottom disk. If we replace the bottom disk with a disk that passes through the top disk, the volume between the two disks is now covered twice. So, no matter how we disentangle these intersecting disks, the volume that was covered twice can now only be covered once. Hence, any disentangling procedure will affect $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ in a complicated way, unlike the area functional.

*Figure 1. The left image depicts the initial stack of two disks. The middle image depicts a replacement for the bottom disk that intersects the top disk. The right image depicts a possible disentanglement of the disks.*

In the course of our proof, we develop two weaker versions of steps (3) and (4). Together, the weak versions of these steps can be used to deduce Theorem 1.1 with sub-optimal $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity.

First weak version. In this version of steps (3) and (4), we deduce the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of the limit of each disk in the stacked disk arrangement.

- (3’) Each disk in a stacked disk arrangement minimizing $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ is itself minimizing for $\mathcal{A}^{\tilde{h}}$ . Using a delicate disentanglement procedure, we find that the limit of each disk is minimizing for $\mathcal{A}^{\tilde{h}}$ , where $\tilde{h}$ is a measurable function bounded by $\sup|h|$ that depends on the limit. We emphasize that $\tilde{h}$ cannot be chosen to be continuous in general.

- (4’) Conclude by Allard’s regularity. Using the same area estimates as step (4), we can apply the theorem of [All72]. However, the first variation of the limit is only known to be $L^{\infty}$ by step (3’), so the limit of each disk is $C^{1,\alpha}$ .

Second weak version. In this version of steps (3) and (4), we determine where the limit is a smooth multiplicity one $h$ -prescribed mean curvature surface and where is it a smooth even multiplicity minimal surface, in the case where $h$ is positive.

- (3”) Reduce the problem of minimizing $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ over many stacked disks in a cylinder to the problem of minimizing $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ over stacked disks with only one or two disks. When $h$ has a sign, it is easier to keep track of volumes under disentanglement. Similar in spirit to step (3) from [AS79], we use this observation in combination with our disentanglement procedure to decompose large stacks of disks into units consisting of only one or two disks (depending on orientations).

- (4”) Conclude by Allard’s regularity. The case of only one stacked disk now follows exactly as in step (4) from [AS79], where we find that the limit is a smooth embedded $h$ -prescribed mean curvature surface. In the two stack case, if the limits of the two disks agree on some open set, we see that the limit is stationary. We then follow step (4) from [AS79] to find that the limit is a smooth embedded minimal surface with multiplicity two.

After deducing the $C^{1,\alpha}$ version of Theorem 1.1, we use some tools from the theory of free boundary problems to upgrade the regularity of our minimizers to $C^{1,1}$ . Indeed, we can show that minimizers locally solve an $n$ -membrane problem for a quasilinear elliptic operator (see [VC74], [Sil05] and [SY19] for more background), to which the recent results of [WZ23b] apply.

#### 1.3. Idea of the proof of existence in the 3-sphere

There are a few key difficulties in carrying over the min-max program of [CDL03] and [DLP10] to our setting, though much remains unchanged. Unique continuation and strong compactness are the two major obstacles.

In the classical min-max settings, unique continuation for surfaces with zero or prescribed mean curvature is used in an essential way to patch together iterated replacements to prove regularity. However, unique continuation does not hold for surfaces with the regularity of Theorem 1.1 (e.g. a multiplicity two minimal surface can suddenly split into two prescribed mean curvature surfaces).

Ignoring the full power of our regularity theory, we overcome the unique continuation issue by finding situations in which min-max solutions and replacement varifolds have density one everywhere. In this case, the regularity of Theorem 1.1 is the same as in the Almgren-Pitts prescribed mean curvature setting (e.g. smooth stable surfaces with prescribed mean curvature). Unique continuation then applies (assuming the prescribing function is sufficiently nice).

To achieve density one, we make two observations about varifolds in the round 3-sphere. First, a varifold limit of a min-max sequence for the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ functional has a mass upper bound (in terms of a bound on the prescribing functional) by comparing with the optimal sweepout for the area functional. Second, a monotonicity formula for the Willmore energy in Euclidean space due to [Sim93] and [Top98] (suitably modified for the varifold setting) gives a lower bound for the mass of a varifold in $S^{3}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}$ with a point of density at least two (in terms of a bound on the first variation). These two bounds contradict when the prescribing function is bounded in absolute value by $0.547$ .

Another essential ingredient in both the regularity theory and genus bounds is a strong compactness theory for minimizers. In the more classical settings, this strong compactness follows from curvature estimates for stable minimal surfaces. Since we only expect $C^{1,1}$ regularity in general, this approach requires special attention. In fact, there is an important and subtle step in the standard point picking contradiction argument for the curvature estimates of stable minimal surfaces that uses the Schauder estimates to upgrade from $C^{1,\alpha}$ convergence to $C^{2}$ convergence. This approach manifestly fails in our setting, because minimizers are not even $C^{2}$ . Instead, we use a $C^{1,1}$ estimate of [WZ23b] for the $n$ -membrane problem that allows us to close the usual point picking argument. This approach supplies a sufficiently strong compactness theorem for the rest of the regularity theory and genus bounds.

#### 1.4. Outline of the paper

In §2, we establish notations and conventions for the rest of the paper. In §3, we carry out the details of two illustrative examples. In Part I, we modify the arguments of [AS79] (e.g. minimizing area over disks) to the the prescribed mean curvature setting. In Part II, we modify the arguments of [MSY82] (e.g. minimizing over isotopy classes) to the prescribed mean curvature setting, and prove Theorem 1.1. In Part III, we develop a strong compactness theory for minimizers with only $C^{1,1}$ regularity. In Part IV, we apply the above regularity theory in the Simon-Smith min-max program to prove Theorems 1.5 and 1.7.

### 2. Notation and Conventions

- • $\mathbb{B}$ denotes $B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(0)$ .

- • $\mathbb{D}$ denotes $\overline{B}_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)$ .

- • $G(U,2)$ denotes the Grassmannian of tangent 2-planes over the set $U\subset M$ .

- • $\mathcal{I}(U)$ is the set of isotopies $\phi:[0,1]\times M\to M$ satisfying

$$ \phi(0,\cdot)=\mathrm{id}\ \ \text{and}\ \ \phi(t,\cdot)|_{M\setminus U}=\mathrm{id}. $$

- • $\mathcal{H}^{n}$ denotes the $n$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure on $(M,g)$ .

- • $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ denots the $h$ -prescribed mean curvature functional; namely, for $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ and a set of finite perimeter $\Omega\subset M$ , we define

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega):=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}. $$

- • $\mathbf{v}(N,m)$ denotes the varifold associated to a $C^{1}$ surface $N\subset M$ with multiplicity $m\in\mathbb{N}$ .

- • $\delta V(X)$ is the first variation of a varifold $V$ with respect to the vector field $X$ . In the case $V$ has bounded first variation, we use the convention

$$ \delta V(X)=\int_{G(M,2)}\mathrm{div}_{\pi}X\ dV(x,\pi)=\int_{M}X\cdot H_{V}\ d\|V\|, $$

where $H_{V}$ is the generalized mean curvature vector of $V$ . We note that with this convention, the unit round sphere $S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ has mean curvature pointing out of the unit ball with length $2$ .

- • $V_{k}\rightharpoonup V$ denotes convergence in the sense of varifolds.

- • $\mu_{k}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}\mu$ denotes weak star convergence in the sense of [Mag12, §4.3].

- • $[\Sigma]$ denotes the integer 2-current associated to an oriented surface $\Sigma$ .

- • $[\Omega]$ denotes the integer 3-current associated to a set of finite perimeter $\Omega$ , oriented so that $\partial[\Omega]$ is the integer 2-current associated to $\partial\Omega$ with orientation given by the outward pointing unit normal.

- • $\mathbb{M}(T)$ denotes the mass of an integral current.

- • $d_{U}$ denotes the distance function from $U$ in $M$ .

- • $U(\theta)$ denotes the set $\{x\in M\mid d_{U}(x)<\theta\}$ .

- • $U_{\xi}$ denotes the set $\{x\in U\mid d(x,\partial U)>\xi\}$ .

### 3. Examples

#### 3.1. Failure of prescribed mean curvature

Here we supply a general class of examples where the limit of any minimizing sequence does not have prescribed mean curvature.

Let $M^{3}=S^{1}\times\Sigma$ where $\Sigma$ is a closed surface. Let $g$ be any metric on $M$ , and $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ any positive function. Let $\Omega_{0}:=I\times\Sigma\subset M$ , where $I$ is an open interval in the $S^{1}$ factor. Let $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ be the components of $\partial\Omega_{0}$ , which are embedded surfaces in the same isotopy class as $\{0\}\times\Sigma\subset M$ . We define

$$ m_{0}:=\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(M)}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(1,\Sigma_{1}))=\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(M)}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(1,\Sigma_{2})). $$

By treating the area and volume terms separately, we see that

$$ \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(M)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega_{0})\geq 2m_{0}-\int_{M}h. $$

Moreover, this lower bound can be achieved by taking a sequence satisfying

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\phi_{k}(1,\Omega_{0})}\xrightarrow{L^{1}}\mathbf{1}_{M} $$

and

$$ \lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi_{k}(1,\Sigma_{1}))=\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi_{k}(1,\Sigma_{2}))=m_{0}. $$

By [MSY82], the varifold limit of the boundaries is a multiplicity 2 stable minimal surface, and therefore does not have prescribed mean curvature $h>0$ .

#### 3.2. Failure of smoothness

We give an example where the limit of any minimizing sequence is not $C^{2}$ . This example is a prototype of the “stacked disk” minimization problem used to prove regularity, which is outlined in the introduction. The failure of smoothness in this example therefore illustrates the essential reason for the failure of smoothness in general.

Let $U:=B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times(-1,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Let

$$ \Omega_{1}:=B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times(-1,-\varepsilon)\ \ \text{and}\ \ \Omega_{2}:=B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times(\varepsilon,1). $$

#### Proposition 3.1.

The problem

$$ \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{c}(\phi(1,\Omega_{1})) $$

has a unique minimizer whose boundary in $U$ is the upward curved spherical cap of radius $2/c$ with boundary $\partial U\cap\{x_{3}=-\varepsilon\}$ .

#### Proof.

We use the calibration technique, see [CM11, Lemma 1.1.1].

Let $\Sigma^{*}$ denote the surface of the upward curved spherical cap of radius $2/c$ with boundary $\partial U\cap\{x_{3}=-\varepsilon\}$ . Let $\Omega_{1}^{*}\subset U$ be the set below $\Sigma^{*}$ in $U$ . It is clear that $\Omega_{1}^{*}=\phi^{*}(1,\Omega_{1})$ for some $\phi^{*}\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ .

Note that $\Sigma^{*}$ is the graph of a function $u$ over $B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)$ . Moreover, $u$ satisfies the mean curvature equation

$$ \mathrm{div}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)=-c. $$

Let $\omega$ be the 2-form given by

$$ \omega(X,Y)=\mathrm{det}(X,Y,\nu), $$

where

$$ \nu:=\frac{(-u_{x},-u_{y},1)}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^{2}}}. $$

By the computation from [CM11, Lemma 1.1.1], we have

$$ \omega=\frac{dx\wedge dy-u_{x}dy\wedge dz-u_{y}dz\wedge dx}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^{2}}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle d\omega \displaystyle=\left[\left(\frac{-u_{x}}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)_{x}+\left(\frac{-u_{y}}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)_{y}\right]dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=c\ dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. $$

Note that $|\omega(X,Y)|\leq 1$ for any pair of orthogonal unit vectors, with equality if and only if $X,Y\in T\Sigma^{*}$ .

Now let $\Omega_{1}^{\prime}=\phi(1,\Omega_{1})$ be any competitor with $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ . Let $\Sigma^{\prime}=\partial\Omega_{1}^{\prime}\cap U$ . Suppose $\Sigma^{\prime}\neq\Sigma^{*}$ . Then by Stokes’ theorem, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{c}(\Omega^{*}) \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{*})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{*}) \displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma^{*}}\omega-\int_{\Omega^{*}}d\omega \displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\omega-\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}d\omega \displaystyle<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{\prime})=\mathcal{A}^{c}(\Omega^{\prime}). $$

The conclusion follows. ∎

By vertical reflection, the analogous statement holds for $\Omega_{2}$ . Fix $c\leq 1$ . Then for $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, we shall see that any minimizer for the problem

$$ \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{c}(\phi(1,\Omega_{1}\cup\Omega_{2})) $$

must have a minimal interface, and therefore cannot be $C^{2}$ .

We give a more precise description of minimizers.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Any minimizer for the problem

$$ \inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{c}(\phi(1,\Omega_{1}\cup\Omega_{2})) $$

is graphical, symmetric under vertical reflection, and rotationally symmetric.

#### Proof.

We first show that minimizers must be graphical. Let $m$ denote the infimum for the above problem (3.1). Let $\Omega^{*}\subset U$ and $V^{*}$ be the Caccioppoli limit and varifold limit respectively of a minimizing sequence. Let $\Omega^{*}_{1}$ and $\Omega^{*}_{2}$ respectively be the limits of $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$ under the isotopies of the minimizing sequence. Then $\Omega^{*}=\Omega_{1}^{*}\cup\Omega_{2}^{*}$ , and

$$ m=\|V^{*}\|(U)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{*})\geq P(\Omega_{1}^{*};U)+P(\Omega_{2}^{*};U)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{1}^{*})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{2}^{*}). $$

Suppose for contradiction that at least one of $\partial\Omega_{1}^{*}\cap U$ or $\partial\Omega_{2}^{*}\cap U$ is not graphical over $B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)$ . For $\mathbf{x}\in B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)$ , let $l_{\mathbf{x}}$ denote the vertical line $\{(\mathbf{x},z)\mid z\in\mathbb{R}\}$ . Consider new sets

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{1}^{\prime}:=\{(\mathbf{x},z)\mid-1<z<\mathcal{H}^{1}(\overline{\Omega^{*}}\cap l_{\mathbf{x}})/2-1\}, \displaystyle\Omega_{2}^{\prime}:=\{(\mathbf{x},z)\mid 1-\mathcal{H}^{1}(\overline{\Omega^{*}}\cap l_{\mathbf{x}})/2<z<1\}. $$

By Steiner symmetrization (see [Mag12, Theorem 14.4]), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{1}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{2}^{\prime})=\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{*})\ \ \text{and}\ \ P(\Omega_{1}^{\prime};U)+P(\Omega_{2}^{\prime};U)\leq P(\Omega_{1}^{*};U)+P(\Omega_{2}^{*};U), $$

where equality holds for the perimeters if and only if $\Omega_{i}^{*}\cap l_{\mathbf{x}}$ is connected for all $\mathbf{x}$ . Hence, we have

$$ P(\Omega_{1}^{\prime};U)+P(\Omega_{2}^{\prime};U)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{1}^{\prime})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{2}^{\prime})<m. $$

Since $\partial\Omega_{i}^{\prime}\cap U$ is graphical over $B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)$ and $\partial\Omega_{i}^{\prime}\setminus U=\partial\Omega_{i}^{*}\setminus U$ by construction, $\Omega^{\prime}:=\Omega_{1}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{2}^{\prime}$ is in the closure of the isotopy class of $\Omega$ (e.g. use a smooth kernel to approximate the boundary of $\Omega_{i}^{\prime}$ by smooth disks with the same boundary), which yields a contradiction.

The proofs of symmetry under reflection and rotation follow similarly by the natural symmetrization procedures. Indeed, these steps are easier, as one can exploit the fact that minimizers are graphical and use the convexity of the function $\sqrt{1+|x|^{2}}$ . ∎

In MATLAB, we programmed a discrete version of the $\mathcal{A}^{1}$ functional for rotationally and vertically symmetric graphs. ## Part I Minimization over disks

We follow the argument of [AS79], with appropriate modifications to the manifold setting as in [MSY82].

### 4. Preliminaries

Let $(M^{3},g)$ be a connected closed55 5 As in [MSY82], we only need to assume that $M$ is homogeneously regular. In this case, we should also assume that $h$ is in $L^{\infty}$ . Riemannian 3-manifold. Let $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function with $c\coloneqq\sup_{M}|h|$ . Before we formulate the minimization problem, we need some preliminary facts about the prescribed mean curvature functional and disks in manifolds.

#### 4.1. Local control

Since $M$ is compact, there are constants $\rho_{0}>0$ , $\mu>0$ , and $\beta_{0}\geq 1$ so that the following hold:

- • For each $x\in M$ , the restriction of the domain and range of $\exp_{x}$ gives a diffeomorphism

$$ \phi_{x}:\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{T_{x}M}(0)\to\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{M}(x). $$

- • For each $\xi\in\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{T_{x}M}(0)$ and $y\in\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{M}(x)$ , we have (4.1)

$$ \|d_{\xi}\phi_{x}\|,\ \|d_{y}\phi_{x}^{-1}\|\leq 2. $$

- • In geodesic normal coordinates $x^{1},x^{2},x^{3}$ for $B_{\rho_{0}}^{M}(x)$ , we have (4.2)

$$ \sup_{\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{T_{x}M}(0)}\left|\frac{\partial g_{ij}}{\partial x^{k}}\right|\leq\mu/\rho_{0},\ \ \sup_{\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{T_{x}M}(0)}\left|\frac{\partial^{2}g_{ij}}{\partial x^{k}\partial x^{l}}\right|\leq\mu/\rho_{0}^{2}. $$

- • For any $\rho\in(0,\rho_{0})$ and $x\in M$ , we have (4.3)

$$ d_{B_{\rho}(x)}\coloneqq\mathrm{dist}(B_{\rho}(x),\cdot)\ \text{is\ convex} $$

on $B_{\rho_{0}}(x)\setminus\overline{B_{\rho}(x)}$ .

- • For any $\rho\in(0,\rho_{0})$ and $x\in M$ , we have (4.4)

$$ \Delta d_{B_{\rho}(x)}\geq c $$

on $B_{\rho_{0}}(x)\setminus\overline{B_{\rho}(x)}$ .

- • For any $\rho\in(0,\rho_{0})$ and $x\in M$ , we have (4.5)

$$ \min\{\mathcal{H}^{2}(E),\ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{\rho}(x)\setminus E)\}\leq\beta_{0}(\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial E))^{2} $$

for any set of finite perimeter $E\subset\partial B_{\rho}(x)$ .

- • For any $0<\rho_{1}<\rho_{2}\leq\rho_{0}$ and $x\in M$ , we have (4.6)

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{\rho_{1}}(x))\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{\rho_{2}}(x)). $$

#### Remark 4.1.

By rescaling the metric and prescribing function, we can assume $\rho_{0}=1$ . We henceforth make this assumption for ease of notation.

#### 4.2. Thin tube isoperimetric inequality

We make frequent use of the following Lemma from [MSY82].

#### Lemma 4.2 ([MSY82, Lemma 1]).

There is a constant $\delta\in(0,1)$ independent of $M$ and $g$ so that if $\Sigma$ is a smooth embedded surface in $M$ and satisfies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma\cap B_{1}(x))<\delta^{2} $$

for all $x\in M$ , then there is a unique compact $K_{\Sigma}\subset M$ with $\partial K_{\Sigma}=\Sigma$ and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Sigma}\cap B_{1}(x))\leq\delta^{3} $$

for all $x\in M$ , and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Sigma})\leq c_{1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)^{3/2}, $$

where $c_{1}=c_{1}(\mu)$ . Moreover, if $\Sigma$ is diffeomorphic to $S^{2}$ , then $K_{\Sigma}$ is diffeomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ .66 6 The exponent of $\delta$ in (4.8) is written as 2 in the statement of [MSY82, Lemma 1], but a quick examination of the proof reveals that it should be 3.

#### 4.3. Area comparison

The following lemma is the appropriate modification of [MSY82, Lemma 3] for our setting. Essentially, we use the divergence theorem to show that moving pieces of a set inside a $c$ -mean convex domain decreases the $\mathcal{A}^{c}$ functional.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $U\subset B_{1/2}(x_{0})$ and $\theta\in(0,1/2)$ satisfy

- • $x_{0}\in U$ ,

- • $\overline{U}$ is diffeomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ ,

- • $d_{U}$ is convex on $U(\theta)\setminus\overline{U}$ ,

- • $\Delta d_{U}\geq c$ on $U(\theta)\setminus\overline{U}$ .

Let $\beta\geq 1$ be a constant so that, for each $s\in(\theta/2,\theta)$ ,

$$ \min\{\mathcal{H}^{2}(E),\ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U(s)\setminus E)\}\leq\beta(\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial E))^{2} $$

whenever $E$ is a surface in $\partial U(s)$ . Let

$$ \delta_{1}=\min\left\{\delta,\ \frac{\theta}{(1+128c_{1})\beta^{1/2}},\ \frac{\theta}{9\beta^{1/2}(1/32+cc_{1})^{1/2}},\ \frac{\mathcal{H}^{3}(M)^{1/3}}{(4c_{1})^{1/3}},\ 1\right\}, $$

(where $c_{1}$ and $\delta$ are as in Lemma 4.2). Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth embedded disk intersecting $\partial U$ transversally with $\partial\Sigma\subset M\setminus U$ . Suppose

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma\setminus U)\leq\delta_{1}^{2}/32. $$

If $\Lambda$ is any component of $\Sigma\setminus U$ with $\partial\Sigma\cap\Lambda=\varnothing$ , then there is a unique compact $K_{\Lambda}\subset M\setminus U$ so that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})\leq c_{1}\delta_{1}^{3},\ \ \partial K_{\Lambda}=\Lambda\cup F, $$

where $F\subset\partial U$ is a surface with $\partial F=\partial\Lambda$ satisfying

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda\cap U(\theta))-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $F_{0}\subset\partial U$ satisfy $\partial F_{0}=\partial\Lambda$ , which exists because $\partial U$ is diffeomorphic to a 2-sphere. Then by (4.11) and (4.12), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{0})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda)<\delta^{2}. $$

By Lemma 4.2, there is a compact set $W\subset M$ with

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(W)\leq c_{1}\delta_{1}^{3},\ \ \partial W=F_{0}\cup\Lambda. $$

Let $K_{\Lambda}=W\setminus U$ , in which case $F$ is either $F_{0}$ (if $W\cap U=\varnothing$ ) or $\partial U\setminus F_{0}$ (if $U\subset W$ ). Since $K_{\Lambda}$ must satisfy $\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})\leq\mathcal{H}^{3}(M)/4$ by the definition of $\delta_{1}$ , $K_{\Lambda}$ is unique.

Define $F_{t}=K_{\Lambda}\cap\partial U(t)$ , $E_{t}=\Lambda\cap U(t)$ , and $K_{t}=K_{\Lambda}\cap U(t)$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{t_{2}}\setminus\overline{K}_{t_{1}}) \displaystyle\leq\int_{K_{t_{2}}\setminus\overline{K}_{t_{1}}}\Delta d_{U} \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t_{2}})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t_{1}})+\int_{\overline{E}_{t_{2}}\setminus E_{t_{1}}}\langle\nu,\nabla d_{U}\rangle \displaystyle\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t_{2}})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t_{1}})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\overline{E}_{t_{2}})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{t_{1}}). $$

Equality in (4.15) requires $E_{t_{1}}=E_{t_{2}}$ , because the identity $\nu(y)=\nabla d_{U}(y)$ for almost every $y\in\overline{E}_{t_{2}}\setminus E_{t_{1}}$ implies $\overline{E}_{t_{2}}\setminus E_{t_{1}}\subset\partial U(s)$ for some $s$ .

By setting $t_{1}=0$ and $t_{2}=t>0$ in (4.15), we get

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\overline{E}_{t})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{t}). $$

If $K_{\theta}=K_{\Lambda}$ , then we obtain (4.14) by setting $t=\theta$ . Henceforth, we assume $K_{\theta}\neq K_{\Lambda}$ .

By the coarea formula, we have

$$ \int_{0}^{\theta}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{s})\ ds\leq\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\theta})\leq c_{1}\delta_{1}^{3}. $$

Hence,

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})\leq 4c_{1}\theta^{-1}\delta_{1}^{3} $$

for a set of $t\in[0,\theta]$ of measure at least $\frac{3}{4}\theta$ . Since $\delta_{1}<(128c_{1})^{-1}\theta$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})\leq\delta_{1}^{2}/32 $$

on a set of measure at least $\frac{3}{4}\theta$ . Then there is a $t^{*}\in[\frac{3}{4}\theta,\theta]$ so that (4.17) holds at $t^{*}$ . Then (4.15) and (4.12) imply

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})\leq\delta_{1}^{2}/32+\delta_{1}^{2}/32=\delta_{1}^{2}/16 $$

for all $t\leq\frac{3}{4}\theta$ .

Since $B_{\theta/2}(x_{0})\subset U(\theta/2)$ and $U(\theta)\subset B_{1}(x_{0})$ , (4.1) and the isoperimetric inequality in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ (since the $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ isoperimetric constant is $\sim 4.8\geq 4$ ) imply

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U(t))\geq\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial(\phi_{x_{0}}^{-1}(U(t))))\geq(\mathcal{H}^{3}(\phi_{x_{0}}^{-1}(B_{\theta/2}(x_{0}))))^{2/3}\geq\theta^{2}/8 $$

for $t\in[\theta/2,\theta]$ . Since $\delta_{1}\leq\theta$ , (4.18) implies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U(t)) $$

for all $t\in[\theta/2,3\theta/4]$ . Then by (4.10) and the coarea formula, we have for almost every $t\in[\theta/2,3\theta/4]$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{t})\leq\beta(\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial F_{t}))^{2}\leq\beta\left(\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{t})\right)^{2}. $$

Hence, (4.16) implies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{t})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})\leq\beta\left(\frac{d}{dt}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(F)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{t})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda}))\right)^{2} $$

for almost every $t\in[\theta/2,3\theta/4]$ . By integration, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathcal{H}^{2}(F)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{\theta/2})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})}- \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathcal{H}^{2}(F)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{3\theta/4})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})}\geq\beta^{-1/2}\theta/8 $$

provided $\mathcal{H}^{2}(F)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{3\theta/4})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})>0$ . By (4.12), (4.13), and (4.11), we have

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathcal{H}^{2}(F)+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\delta_{1}^{2}/32+cc_{1}\delta_{1}^{3}} \displaystyle\leq\delta_{1}\sqrt{1/32+cc_{1}} \displaystyle\leq\beta^{-1/2}\theta/9, $$

so we reach a contradiction. Hence, we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{3\theta/4})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda})<\mathcal{H}^{2}(E_{\theta})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K_{\Lambda}), $$

as desired. ∎

### 5. Minimization Problem

In this section, we rigorously formulate the problem of minimizing the prescribed mean curvature functional over disks in a manifold.

#### 5.1. Setup

Let $c_{1}$ and $\delta$ as in Lemma 4.2. As in the statement of Lemma 4.3, we define

$$ \delta_{2}\coloneqq\min\left\{\delta,\ \frac{\rho_{0}/2}{(1+128c_{1})\beta_{0}^{1/2}},\ \frac{\rho_{0}/2}{9\beta_{0}^{1/2}(1/32+cc_{1})^{1/2}},\ \frac{\mathcal{H}^{3}(M)^{1/3}}{(4c_{1})^{1/3}},\ 1\right\}, $$

where $\rho_{0}$ and $\beta_{0}$ are defined in §4.1.

Let $U\subset B_{1/2}(x_{0})$ and $\theta\in(0,1/2)$ satisfy

- • $x_{0}\in U$ ,

- • $\overline{U}$ is diffeomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ (denoted by $\overline{U}\approx\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ ),

- • $d_{U}$ is convex on $U(\theta)\setminus\overline{U}$ ,

- • $\Delta d_{U}\geq c$ on $U(\theta)\setminus\overline{U}$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U)<\delta_{2}^{2}/32$ .

Let $\beta$ and $\delta_{1}$ be defined in terms of $U$ and $\theta$ as in Lemma 4.3. Note that by (4.3), (4.4), (4.5), there are valid choices $U$ and $\theta$ so that $\delta_{2}\leq\delta_{1}$ (e.g. we can take $U=B_{\rho}(x_{0})$ for $\rho\ll\rho_{0}/2$ and $\theta=\rho_{0}/2$ ).

We define the following notation.

- • $\mathcal{D}$ is the set of oriented smooth embedded 2-disks $\Sigma\subset M$ with smooth boundary.

- • $[\Sigma]$ is the integral $2$ -current corresponding to $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}$ .

- • $\mathcal{D}[\Sigma]$ is the set of disks $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}$ with $\partial[\Sigma^{\prime}]=\partial[\Sigma]$ .

- • $\mathcal{D}(U)$ is the set of disks $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}$ so that – $\partial\Sigma\cap U=\varnothing$ , – $\Sigma$ has transverse (or empty) intersection with $\partial U$ , – there is an open set $\Omega\subset U$ so that $\partial[\Omega]\llcorner U=[\Sigma]\llcorner U$ .

- • $\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ is the set of disks $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}(U)$ so that – $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma\setminus U)\leq\delta_{1}^{2}/32$ , – $\partial\Sigma\setminus\partial U$ is not contained in $K_{\Lambda}$ for any component $\Lambda$ of $\Sigma\setminus U$ with $\partial\Sigma\cap\Lambda=\varnothing$ , where $K_{\Lambda}$ is as in Lemma 4.3.

- • $\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ is the set of $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)\cap\mathcal{D}[\Sigma]$ satisfying – $\Sigma^{\prime}\setminus U\subset\Sigma\setminus U$ , – if $x\in\Sigma^{\prime}\setminus U$ , then $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^{\prime}$ have the same orientation at $x$ .

We note that if $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ then $\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]\subset\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ .

#### 5.2. Fill-ins

The prescribed mean curvature functional requires integration over a region. We formulate these regions here.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ and $\Sigma_{1},\ \Sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ . There is a unique integral 3-current $T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})$ satisfying

$$ \partial T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})=[\Sigma_{1}]-[\Sigma_{2}]\ \ \text{and}\ \ \mathrm{spt}(T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}))\subset\overline{U}\cup\bigcup_{\Lambda}K_{\Lambda}, $$

where $\Lambda$ are the components of $\Sigma\setminus U$ with $\Lambda\cap\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ , and $K_{\Lambda}$ is the corresponding set from Lemma 4.3.

#### Proof.

Let $K\coloneqq\overline{U}\cup\bigcup_{\Lambda}K_{\Lambda}$ . Note that there is a 3-current $S$ with $\mathrm{spt}(S)\subset K$ obtained by adding $\pm[K_{\Lambda}]$ for each $\Lambda\subset\Sigma_{i}$ for some $i$ with the appropriate sign so that

$$ \mathrm{spt}([\Sigma_{1}]-[\Sigma_{2}]-\partial S)\subset\overline{U}. $$

Since $\overline{U}$ is diffeomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ and $H_{2}(\overline{\mathbb{B}},\mathbb{Z})=0$ , there is a current $T$ with support in $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ so that

$$ [\Sigma_{1}]-[\Sigma_{2}]=\partial(S+T). $$

We take $T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}):=S+T$ . The uniqueness follows by the fact there are no nonzero closed 3-currents in $M$ with support in $K$ . ∎

#### Definition 5.2.

We call $T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})$ from Proposition 5.1 the fill-in of $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ . We let $F:I_{3}(M,\mathbb{Z})\to L^{1}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ denote the canonical isomorphism of normed linear spaces, and we define the fill-in integral as

$$ T_{h}(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})\coloneqq\int_{M}h\ F(T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}))\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}. $$

#### Proposition 5.3.

Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ . For $\Sigma_{1},\ \Sigma_{2},\ \Sigma_{3}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}) \displaystyle=-T(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{1}), \displaystyle T_{h}(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}) \displaystyle=-T_{h}(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{1}), $$

$$ \displaystyle T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})+T(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{3}) \displaystyle=T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{3}), \displaystyle T_{h}(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})+T_{h}(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{3}) \displaystyle=T_{h}(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{3}). $$

#### Proof.

We compute

$$ \partial(-T(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{1}))=-[\Sigma_{2}]+[\Sigma_{1}]. $$

By the uniqueness of $T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})$ , (5.4) follows.

We compute

$$ \partial(T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2})+T(\Sigma_{2},\Sigma_{3}))=[\Sigma_{1}]-[\Sigma_{2}]+[\Sigma_{2}]-[\Sigma_{3}]=[\Sigma_{1}]-[\Sigma_{3}]. $$

By the uniqueness of $T(\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{3})$ , (5.5) follows. ∎

#### 5.3. Problem formulation

In this part of the paper, we consider the following question.

#### Question 5.4.

If $\{\Sigma_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ satisfies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma_{k},\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $\Sigma_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma_{k}]$ with $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ , does (a subsequence of) $\Sigma_{k}$ converge to a regular limit with prescribed mean curvature $h$ ?

### 6. Limits of Minimizing Sequences

We apply the standard theory for sets of finite perimeter to deduce some basic preliminary conclusions about the limit in Question 5.4. In later sections we upgrade these basic observations to stronger regularity results.

#### Theorem 6.1.

Suppose $\{\Sigma_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ satisfies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma_{k},\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $\Sigma_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma_{k}]$ with $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ . Let $\Omega_{k}\subset U$ be the open set satisfying

$$ \partial[\Omega_{k}]\llcorner U=[\Sigma_{k}]\llcorner U. $$

If $\sup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap U)<\infty$ , then there is a subsequence (not relabeled), a set of finite perimeter $\Omega\subset U$ , and a varifold $V$ in $U$ so that

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{k}}\xrightarrow{L^{1}}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{k}}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ \mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k}\cap U)\rightharpoonup V. $$

Furthermore,

- • $\Omega$ and $V$ satisfy (6.2)

$$ \|V\|(U)-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\|\phi_{\#}V\|(U)-\int_{\phi(\Omega)}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} $$

for any diffeomorphism $\phi$ of $U$ equal to the identity outside a compact subset of $U$ .

- • the first variation of $V$ satisfies (6.3)

$$ \delta V(X)=\int_{\partial^{*}\Omega}X\cdot h\nu_{\partial^{*}\Omega}\ d|D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega}| $$

for any $C^{1}$ vector field $X$ with $\mathrm{spt}(X)\subset\subset U$ .

- • $V$ has $c$ -bounded first variation, in the sense that (6.4)

$$ \|\delta V\|(B_{r}(x))\leq c\|V\|(B_{r}(x)) $$

for all $B_{r}(x)\subset U$ .

- • The function (6.5)

$$ r\mapsto f(r)\frac{\|V\|(B_{r}(x))}{\pi r^{2}} $$

is monotone increasing in $r$ , where $f$ is a continuous function depending only on $c$ and $(M,g)$ satisfying $f(r)\to 1$ as $r\to 0$ .

#### Proof.

The subsequential convergence follows by the standard compactness theorems (see [Mag12, Theorem 12.26] and [Sim83, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.4]).

Let $\phi$ be a diffeomorphism of $U$ equal to the identity outside a compact subset. The assumption of transverse intersection implies

- (1) $\lim_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap U)=\|V\|(U)$ ,

- (2) $\lim_{k}\int_{\Omega_{k}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}=\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}$ ,

- (3) $\lim_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(\Sigma_{k})\cap U)=\|\phi_{\#}V\|(U)$ ,

- (4) $\lim_{k}\int_{\phi(\Omega_{k})}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}=\int_{\phi(\Omega)}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}$ .

Let $\delta>0$ . Then there exists $k$ sufficiently large so that

$$ \displaystyle\|V\|(U)-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap U)-\int_{\Omega_{k}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}+2\delta \displaystyle(1)+(2) \displaystyle\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(\Sigma_{k})\cap U)-\int_{\phi(\Omega_{k})}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}+3\delta \displaystyle(\ref{eqn:min_seq_compactness}) \displaystyle\leq\|\phi_{\#}V\|(U)-\int_{\phi(\Omega)}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}+5\delta \displaystyle(3)+(4). $$

Since $\delta$ is arbitrary, (6.2) follows.

For a $C^{1}$ vector field $X$ with $\mathrm{spt}(X)\subset\subset U$ , (6.2) and [Mag12, Proposition 17.8] imply

$$ \displaystyle\delta V(X) \displaystyle=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\|(\phi_{t})_{\#}V\|(U) \displaystyle=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\int_{\phi_{t}(\Omega)}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle=\int_{\partial^{*}\Omega}X\cdot h\nu_{\partial^{*}\Omega}\ d|D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega}|, $$

where $\phi_{t}$ is the flow of $X$ . Hence, (6.3) holds.

(6.4) follows from (6.3) and [Mag12, Proposition 4.30].

Finally, the monotonicity of (6.5) follows from (6.4) by [Sim83, Chapter 8, Section 40]77 7 We note that [Sim83] only finds a monotonicity formula for varifolds in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ . We can isometrically embed $(M,g)$ in some $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ and use this monotonicity formula, in which case the function $f$ will depend on the norm of the second fundamental form of the embedding.. ∎

### 7. Resolution of Overlaps

We prove the appropriate modification of [AS79, Lemma 2 and Corollary 1] in our setting, to disentangle overlapping disks. The key difference is that we must keep track of volumes in addition to area.

#### 7.1. Lipschitz disks

As in [AS79], we define a specific class of Lipschitz disks. Fix an open set $U\subset M$ .

#### Definition 7.1.

Consider $n$ disjoint copies $\{F_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ of $\mathbb{D}$ and define $\mathcal{Y}$ to be the collection of Lipschitz maps $\chi:\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}F_{i}\to U$ such that:

- (1) there are finitely many (or zero) pairwise disjoint $C^{2}$ Jordan curves $\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{m}\subset U$ such that for each $k=1,\dots,m$ ,

$$ \chi^{-1}(\Gamma_{k})=\gamma_{k}^{1}\cup\gamma_{k}^{2}, $$

where $\{\gamma_{k}^{l}:k=1,\dots,m;\ l=1,2\}$ is a collection of $2m$ pairwise disjoint $C^{2}$ Jordan curves in $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}(F_{i}\setminus\partial F_{i})$ , and $\chi|_{\gamma_{k}^{l}}$ is a $C^{2}$ parametrization of $\Gamma_{k}$ .

- (2) the restriction of $\chi$ to $\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}F_{i}\right)\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{m}(\gamma_{k}^{1}\cup\gamma_{k}^{2})$ is a $C^{2}$ embedding into $U$ .

- (3) for each $k=1,\dots,m$ , there exist disjoint tubular neighborhoods $W_{k}^{1}$ , $W_{k}^{2}$ of $\gamma_{k}^{1}$ , $\gamma_{k}^{2}$ respectively, such that $\chi(W_{k}^{1})\cap\chi(W_{k}^{2})=\Gamma_{k}$ and exactly one of the following holds: (3a) $\chi(W_{k}^{1})$ lies on one side of $\chi(W_{k}^{2})$ , (3b) $\chi(W_{k}^{1})$ intersects $\chi(W_{k}^{2})$ transversely along $\Gamma_{k}$ .

For future convenience, let us introduce the following notation. For each $k=1,\dots,m$ and $l=1,2$ , let $W_{k}^{l,+}=(W_{k}^{l}\cap\intr(\gamma_{k}^{l}))\setminus\gamma_{k}^{l}$ and $W_{k}^{l,-}=W_{k}^{l}\setminus(W_{k}^{l,+}\cup\gamma_{k}^{l})$ , so that $W_{k}^{l}=W_{k}^{l,+}\cup\gamma_{k}^{l}\cup W_{k}^{l,-}$ .

Finally, define $\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ to be the collection of Lipschitz maps $\chi\in\mathcal{Y}$ such that only (3a) occurs for all $k=1,\dots,m$ . These are the “disentangled” disks, so our goal will be to change a map in $\mathcal{Y}$ into a map in $\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ .

#### Remark 7.2.

As in [AS79], notice that $\chi\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}F_{i}\setminus\partial F_{i}\right)\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\Gamma_{i}$ is a 2-dimensional open submanifold of $M$ , each component of which has closure of the form $\chi(\overline{R})$ , where $R$ is a component of $\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}F_{i}\right)\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{m}(\gamma_{k}^{1}\cup\gamma_{k}^{2})$ .

We will say a finite collection $\mathcal{S}$ of Lipschitz disks is in $\mathcal{Y}$ (or $\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ ), and write $\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{Y}$ (or $\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ ), if it is the image of some map $\chi\in\mathcal{Y}$ (or $\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ , respectively).

#### 7.2. Resolution procedure

We develop a procedure to disentangle intersecting disks by swapping pieces without changing the image of the union of the disks.

#### Lemma 7.3 (Resolution of Overlaps).

Let $U\subset M$ be a bounded connected open set with $C^{1}$ boundary. Let $\mathcal{S}=\{D_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{Y}$ . Then there are Lipschitz disks $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}=\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ with $\tilde{D}_{i}\subset U$ and $\partial\tilde{D}_{i}=\partial D_{i}$ satisfying

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{D}_{i}. $$

#### Proof.

We use notation as in Definition 7.1.

For each intersection curve $\Gamma_{k}$ , exactly one of (3a) and (3b) in Definition 7.1 holds. Let

$$ \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})=\{1\leq k\leq m\mid\text{(3b) occurs}\}. $$

If $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})=\varnothing$ , then $\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ and we are done. Hence, it suffices by induction to furnish a procedure which replaces the collection $\mathcal{S}$ of disks with another collection $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathcal{Y}$ such that:

- • $\bigcup_{i}D_{i}=\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ ,

- • $\partial\tilde{D}_{i}=\partial D_{i}$ ,

- • $|\mathcal{B}(\tilde{\mathcal{S}})|<|\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})|$ .

Let $q\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})$ . There are (without loss of generality) two cases to consider.

Case 1: $\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}\cap\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2}=\varnothing$ . Fix a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism

$$ \psi_{q}:\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}}\to\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2}} $$

so that $(\chi\circ\psi_{q})|_{\gamma_{q}^{1}}=\chi|_{\gamma_{q}^{2}}$ . Then we define a bijection $\Psi_{q}:\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}\to\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}$ by

$$ \Psi_{q}(\xi)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\psi_{q}(\xi)&\xi\in\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}}\\
\psi_{q}^{-1}(\xi)&\xi\in\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2}}\\
\xi&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Case 2: $\gamma_{q}^{2}\subset\text{int}(\gamma_{q}^{1})$ . Fix a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism

$$ \psi_{q}:\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}}\setminus\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2}\to\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}}\setminus\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2} $$

so that $(\chi\circ\psi_{q})|_{\gamma_{q}^{l}}=\chi|_{\gamma_{q}^{l+1}}$ (where the superscripts are taken mod 2 for convenience). Then we define a bijection $\Psi_{q}:\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}\to\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}$ by

$$ \Psi_{q}(\xi)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\psi_{q}(\xi)&\xi\in\overline{\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{1}}\setminus\text{int}\gamma_{q}^{2}\\
\xi&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

We define $\tilde{\chi}\coloneqq\chi\circ\Psi_{q}:\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}\to M$ . By the boundary assumption, in either case, $\tilde{\chi}$ is a Lipschitz map. Since $\Psi_{q}$ is a bijection, $\tilde{\chi}$ has the same image as $\chi$ . Moreover, $\tilde{\chi}$ agrees with $\chi$ in a neighborhood of the boundaries of the $F_{i}$ . Note that the restriction

$$ \Psi_{q}:\left(\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}\right)\setminus(\gamma_{q}^{1}\cup\gamma_{q}^{2})\to\left(\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i}\right)\setminus(\gamma_{q}^{1}\cup\gamma_{q}^{2}) $$

is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism. We check each component of Definition 7.1:

- (1) Since $\Psi_{q}$ is a bijection, we have $\tilde{\chi}^{-1}(\Gamma_{k})=\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{1}\cup\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{2}$ , where $\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{l}\coloneqq\Psi_{q}^{-1}(\gamma_{k}^{l})$ are disjoint sets. Since $\Psi_{q}$ is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism away from $\gamma_{q}^{1}\cup\gamma_{q}^{2}$ , $\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{l}$ is a $C^{2}$ Jordan curve for all $k\neq q$ and $\tilde{\chi}|_{\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{l}}$ is a $C^{2}$ parametrization. Finally, it follows from the construction that $\tilde{\gamma}_{q}^{l}=\gamma_{q}^{l+1}$ and $\tilde{\chi}|_{\tilde{\gamma}_{q}^{l}}$ is a $C^{2}$ parametrization.

- (2) Since $\Psi_{q}$ is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism away from $\tilde{\gamma}_{q}^{1}\cup\tilde{\gamma}_{q}^{2}$ , the restriction of $\tilde{\chi}$ to any component of $(\bigsqcup_{i}F_{i})\setminus(\bigsqcup_{k}\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{1}\cup\tilde{\gamma}_{k}^{2})$ is a $C^{2}$ embedding.

- (3) For $k\neq q$ , the desired tubular neighborhoods are $\tilde{W}_{k}^{l}=\Psi_{q}^{-1}(W_{k}^{l})$ . Since $\tilde{\chi}(\tilde{W}_{k}^{l})=\chi(W_{k}^{l})$ , (3a) (resp. (3b)) holds at $k\neq q$ for $\tilde{\chi}$ if and only if (3a) (resp. (3b)) holds at $k$ for $\chi$ . We now define $\tilde{W}_{q}^{l}$ , which differ in the above cases. • In Case 1, we have

$$ \tilde{W}_{q}^{l}=\Psi_{q}^{-1}(W_{q}^{l,-}\cup\gamma_{q}^{l+1}\cup W_{q}^{l+1,+}). $$

Then

$$ \tilde{\chi}(\tilde{W}_{q}^{l})=\chi(W_{q}^{l,-})\cup\Gamma_{q}\cup\chi(W_{q}^{l+1,+}) $$

• In Case 2, we have $\displaystyle\tilde{W}_{q}^{1}$ $\displaystyle=\Psi_{q}^{-1}(W_{q}^{1,-}\cup\gamma_{q}^{2}\cup W_{q}^{2,-})$ $\displaystyle\tilde{W}_{q}^{2}$ $\displaystyle=\Psi_{q}^{-1}(W_{q}^{2,+}\cup\gamma_{q}^{1}\cup W_{q}^{1,+}).$ Then $\displaystyle\tilde{\chi}(\tilde{W}_{q}^{1})$ $\displaystyle=\chi(W_{q}^{1,-})\cup\Gamma_{q}\cup\chi(W_{q}^{2,-})$ $\displaystyle\tilde{\chi}(\tilde{W}_{q}^{2})$ $\displaystyle=\chi(W_{q}^{2,+})\cup\Gamma_{q}\cup\chi(W_{q}^{1,+}).$ Since (3b) holds at $q$ for $\chi$ , we see that (3a) holds at $q$ for $\tilde{\chi}$ .

Hence, $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}$ . Moreover, it follows from (3) above that $|\mathcal{B}(\tilde{\mathcal{S}})|<|\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})|$ . ∎

#### Remark 7.4.

The procedure described in the proof of Lemma 7.3 is not uniquely determined by the initial collection $\mathcal{S}$ . However, we will see that this is not an issue in our applications.

After applying the resolution procedure, we will make small perturbations to produce genuinely embedded surfaces. We collect the required statements in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 7.5.

Let $U\subset M$ be an open set with $\overline{U}\approx\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ . Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}(U)$ . Let $\{D_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be a set of smooth embedded disks with $D_{i}\subset U$ , $\partial D_{i}\subset\partial U$ , and

$$ \Sigma\cap U=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}. $$

Let $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ satisfy $\tilde{D}_{i}\subset U$ and $\partial[\tilde{D}_{i}]=\partial[D_{i}]$ . Then there is an open set $\tilde{\Omega}\subset U$ satisfying

$$ \partial[\tilde{\Omega}]\llcorner U=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\tilde{D}_{i}]. $$

Moreover, for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is a $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ satisfying

$$ \Sigma\triangle\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{D}_{i})+\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})-([\Omega]-[\tilde{\Omega}]))\leq\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

The existence of $\tilde{\Omega}$ follows from the existence of $\Omega$ and the fact that the boundary orientations of the disks agree.

The remaining conclusions follow from making small perturbations along the intersection curves of the disks $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}$ . ∎

#### 7.3. Application 1: Collapsing to the boundary

As a first application of the resolution procedure, we would like to ignore some components of a minimizing sequence in a ball by collapsing those components to the boundary of the ball.

#### Lemma 7.6.

Let $U\subset M$ be an open set with $\overline{U}\approx\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ . Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}(U)$ . Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of smooth embedded disks $D$ with $D\subset U$ , $\partial D\subset\partial U$ , and

$$ \Sigma\cap U=\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}}D. $$

Let $\mathcal{S}_{0}\subset\mathcal{S}$ . For $D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ , let $F_{D}\subset\partial U$ be the isoperimetric region for $\partial D$ , and let $\Lambda_{D}$ be the region in $U$ bounded by $D\cup F_{D}$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ satisfying

$$ \Sigma\triangle\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U)\leq\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D})+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{0}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime}))\leq\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D})+\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

To apply Lemma 7.3, we must first perturb the disks $F_{D}$ . Let $\eta>0$ so that $\mathcal{H}^{3}(B_{\eta}(\partial U))<\varepsilon/2$ . We define disks $F_{D}^{\prime}$ for $D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ so that the following hold:

- • $F_{D_{1}}^{\prime}\cap F_{D_{2}}^{\prime}=\varnothing$ for $D_{1}\neq D_{2}\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ ,

- • $F_{D_{1}}$ has transverse (or empty) intersection with $D_{2}$ for any $D_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ and $D_{2}\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{0}$ ,

- • $F_{D}^{\prime}\subset U$ and $\partial F_{D}^{\prime}=\partial D$ ,

- • $|\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D}^{\prime})|<\varepsilon/(2|\mathcal{S}_{0}|)$ ,

- • $F_{D}^{\prime}\subset B_{\eta}(\partial U)\cap\Lambda_{D}$ .

We can then apply Lemma 7.3 to the disks

$$ \mathcal{S}^{\prime}\coloneqq(\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{0})\cup\{F_{D}^{\prime}\}_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}, $$

producing a collection $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ .

By Lemma 7.5 and the choice of $\eta$ , it then suffices show (up to a set of $\mathcal{H}^{3}$ measure zero)

$$ (\Omega\triangle\tilde{\Omega})\setminus B_{\eta}(\partial U)\subset\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}\Lambda_{D}. $$

Let $x\in(\Omega\triangle\tilde{\Omega})\setminus B_{\eta}(\partial U)$ . Take a point

$$ x_{0}\in\partial U\setminus\left(\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}F_{D}\cup\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}}\partial D\right). $$

We also assume $x$ is not in any $D\in\mathcal{S}$ or $\tilde{D}\in\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ , which is a set of $\mathcal{H}^{3}$ measure zero. Let $\gamma:(0,1]\to U$ be a smooth path having transverse intersection with any $D\in\mathcal{S}$ or $\tilde{D}\in\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ , satisfying $\lim_{t\to 0}\gamma(t)=x_{0}$ and $\gamma(1)=x$ . Since $x_{0}$ and $x$ are in the complement of $B_{\eta}(\partial U)\cap(\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}}\overline{\Lambda}_{D})$ , which contains the disks $F_{D}^{\prime}$ , we conclude that $\gamma$ intersects each $F_{D}^{\prime}$ for $D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ an even number of times. Since $x\in\Omega\triangle\tilde{\Omega}$ and $x_{0}\notin\overline{\Omega\triangle\tilde{\Omega}}$ , we conclude that $\gamma$ intersects some $D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ an odd number of times. Since $x_{0}\notin\overline{\Lambda}_{D}$ , we have $x\in\Lambda_{D}$ for some $D\in\mathcal{S}_{0}$ . ∎

#### 7.4. Application 2: Isolating one stacked disk

Our goal in this application is to isolate individual disks in a stacked disk minimization problem to deduce some (albeit weaker) regularity for each sheet of the limit varifold.

We first establish some notation.

Let $U\approx\mathbb{B}$ satisfy $\partial U=\overline{C}\cup\overline{D^{+}}\cup\overline{D^{-}}$ , where $C$ is a smoothly embedded annulus and $D^{+}$ and $D^{-}$ are smoothly embedded disks. Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}(U)$ , in the sense that $\Sigma\cap\partial C=\varnothing$ . Moreover, assume $\Sigma\cap U$ is a disjoint union of smooth embedded oriented disks $\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}\}$ , each of which has homotopically nontrivial boundary in $C$ .

For $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , let $B_{i}\subset U$ be the open subset satisfying

$$ D^{-}\subset\partial B_{i}\setminus D_{i}\subset\partial U. $$

If $B_{i}\subset B_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ , we say $D_{i}<D_{j}$ . Without loss of generality, we suppose

$$ D_{1}>D_{2}>\ldots>D_{n}. $$

Let $\Omega_{i}\subset U$ be the open subset satisfying

$$ \partial[\Omega_{i}]\llcorner U=[D_{i}]\llcorner U. $$

If $B_{i}=\Omega_{i}$ , we say $D_{i}$ is oriented up. Otherwise, we say $D_{i}$ is oriented down. By the ordering of the $D_{i}$ and the fact that $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}(U)$ , $D_{i}$ is oriented up if and only if $D_{i-1}$ and $D_{i+1}$ are oriented down (i.e. the orientation alternates with respect to the ordering).

#### Lemma 7.7.

Fix some $1\leq j\leq n$ . Let $D_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[D_{j}]$ so that $D_{j}^{\prime}$ has transverse intersections with each $D_{i}$ for $i\neq j$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ satisfying

$$ \Sigma\triangle\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j}^{\prime})+\sum_{i\neq j}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{i})+\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})-[\Omega^{+}]+[\Omega^{-}])\leq\varepsilon, $$

where $\Omega^{+}$ and $\Omega^{-}$ are disjoint sets contained in $\Omega_{j}\triangle\Omega_{j}^{\prime}$ .

Moreover, instead of (7.10), we can construct $\Sigma^{\prime}$ satisfying

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})-([\Omega_{j}]-[\Omega_{j}^{\prime}])-[(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega]+G)\leq\varepsilon. $$

where $G$ is a nonnegative integral current, in the sense that $\int F(G)f\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\geq 0$ for all nonnegative $f$ .

#### Proof.

Step 1: We apply Lemma 7.3 to the disks $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\coloneqq\{D_{j}^{\prime}\}\cup\{D_{i}\}_{i\neq j}$ , producing new disks $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}=\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ .

We claim

$$ [\Omega]-[\tilde{\Omega}]=[\Omega_{j}]-[\Omega_{j}^{\prime}]+2[(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega]-2[(\Omega_{j}\setminus\Omega_{j}^{\prime})\setminus\Omega], $$

which implies (7.10) by Lemma 7.5 and taking

$$ \displaystyle\Omega^{+}:=(\Omega_{j}\triangle\Omega_{j}^{\prime})\cap\Omega,\ \ \Omega^{-}:=(\Omega_{j}\triangle\Omega_{j}^{\prime})\setminus\Omega. $$

We first observe

$$ \displaystyle[\Omega]-[\tilde{\Omega}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\Omega_{i}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\tilde{\Omega}_{i}]=([\Omega_{j}]-[\Omega_{j}^{\prime}])+\left([\Omega_{j}^{\prime}]+\sum_{i\neq j}[\Omega_{i}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\tilde{\Omega}_{i}]\right). $$

Let

$$ \tilde{N}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\tilde{\Omega}_{i}},\ \ N^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j}^{\prime}}+\sum_{i\neq j}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{i}}. $$

To show (7.12), it suffices to show for $\mathcal{H}^{3}$ -a.e. $x\in U$ that

$$ N^{\prime}(x)-\tilde{N}(x)=\begin{cases}2&x\in(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega\\
-2&x\in(\Omega_{j}\setminus\Omega_{j}^{\prime})\setminus\Omega\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Let $R$ be the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}D_{i}$ containing $x$ . Let $x_{0}\in C\cap\overline{R}$ . Let $\gamma:(0,1]\to U$ be a path in $R$ so that

- • $\gamma$ avoids the intersection curves $\{\Gamma_{k}\}$ ,

- • $\gamma$ has transverse intersection with $D_{j}^{\prime}$ ,

- • $\lim_{t\to 0}\gamma(t)=x_{0}$ and $\gamma(1)=x$ .

We have $N^{\prime}(x_{0})=\tilde{N}(x_{0})$ . Along subsequent intersections of $\gamma$ with $D_{j}^{\prime}$ , each of $N^{\prime}$ and $\tilde{N}$ will increase and decrease by 1 in alternating order.

If $\gamma$ has an even number of intersections with $D_{j}^{\prime}$ , then we see $N^{\prime}(x)=\tilde{N}(x)$ . Hence, we only need to consider the case of an odd number of intersections, which is equivalent to $x\in\Omega_{j}\triangle\Omega_{j}^{\prime}$ . In this case, $N^{\prime}$ increases at the first intersection if and only if $x\in\Omega_{j}^{\prime}$ . Note that $\tilde{N}$ decreases at the first intersection if and only if $R\subset\Omega$ . Hence, (7.13) follows.

Step 2: We further modify the disks $\tilde{D}_{i}$ to $\tilde{D}_{i}^{\prime}$ so that (up to a current with arbitrarily small mass)

$$ [\tilde{\Omega}]-[\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}]=-[(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega]-G, $$

where $G$ is a nonnegative integral current, which implies (7.11) by (7.12) and Lemma 7.5.

Let $R$ be a component of $(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega$ . We collect the following facts.

- (1) $R\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ : a direct consequence of (7.12).

- (2) $\partial R\cap\partial U=\varnothing$ : follows from $\partial\Omega_{j}\cap\partial U=\partial\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\cap\partial U$ .

- (3) $R$ is a component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ : Let $x,\ y\in R$ . By definition, there is a path $\alpha$ from $x$ to $y$ contained in both $\Omega$ and in $\Omega_{j}^{\prime}$ , so $\alpha$ does not intersect any of the disks $\{D_{i}\}$ nor $D_{j}^{\prime}$ . Moreover, since $D_{j}\cap\overline{\Omega\setminus\Omega_{j}}=\varnothing$ , we have $\partial R\subset\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ .

Let $\tilde{\chi}:\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}F_{i}\to M$ be the Lipschitz map corresponding to the resolved disks $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ . Let $\{\sigma_{l}\}_{l}\subset\{\Gamma_{k}\}_{k}$ be the components of $\partial(\tilde{\chi}^{-1}(\partial R))$ . Choose some $\sigma\in\{\sigma_{l}\}$ so that $\sigma\not\subset\text{int}(\sigma_{l})$ for any $l$ . By Definition 7.1, there is a unique distinct curve $\sigma^{\prime}\in\{\Gamma_{k}\}_{k}$ so that $\tilde{\chi}(\sigma)=\tilde{\chi}(\sigma^{\prime})$ . There are two cases.

Case 1: $\text{int}\sigma\cap\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}=\varnothing$ . Since $d_{1}\coloneqq\tilde{\chi}(\overline{\text{int}\sigma})$ and $d_{2}\coloneqq\tilde{\chi}(\overline{\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}})$ are Lipschitz disks with a common boundary and that do not cross through each other, there is a unique open set $R^{\prime}\subset U$ with $\partial R^{\prime}=d_{1}\cup d_{2}$ .

We claim that the disks $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}$ do not intersect $R^{\prime}$ . Suppose otherwise for contradiction. Then for some $i$ there is an $x\in F_{i}\setminus(\overline{\text{int}\sigma\cup\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}})$ satisfying $\tilde{\chi}(x)\in R^{\prime}$ . Let $\alpha$ be a path in $F_{i}\setminus(\overline{\text{int}\sigma\cup\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}})$ from $x$ to $\partial F_{i}$ . Then we have $\tilde{\chi}(\alpha(0))\in R^{\prime}$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\alpha(1))\notin R^{\prime}$ . Since $\partial R^{\prime}=d_{1}\cup d_{2}$ , we conclude that $\tilde{D}_{i}$ crosses through one of $d_{1}$ or $d_{2}$ , which contradicts $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ .

We claim that $R\subset R^{\prime}$ . We consider the local picture along $\tilde{\chi}(\sigma)$ , where the 4 pieces $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ , $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ , $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ , and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ intersect with an X cross-section. We have

- • $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ are adjacent: follows from $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ .

- • $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ are adjacent: follows from the definition of $R^{\prime}$ and the fact that $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}$ do not intersect $R^{\prime}$ .

$R^{\prime}$ contains the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ contained between $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ along this intersection. Since $R$ touches $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and does not touch $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ , fact (3) above implies that $R$ is the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ contained between $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ along this intersection. Hence, $R\subset R^{\prime}$ .

We claim that $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ . Since $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ , each component of $R^{\prime}$ touches the same side of each of $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ . By the definition of $\tilde{\Omega}$ , we have either $R^{\prime}\subset\tilde{\Omega}$ or $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ . By fact (1) above, we have $R\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ , so $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}^{c}\neq\varnothing$ . Hence, $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ .

Collapse procedure: Relabel $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{\prime}$ as $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ so that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}\sigma_{1}))\geq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}\sigma_{2})). $$

Fix a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism

$$ \psi:\overline{\text{int}\sigma_{1}}\to\overline{\text{int}\sigma_{2}} $$

so that $(\tilde{\chi}\circ\psi)|_{\sigma_{1}}=\tilde{\chi}|_{\sigma_{2}}$ . Then we define the map

$$ \tilde{\chi}^{\prime}(\xi)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\tilde{\chi}(\psi(\xi))&\xi\in\overline{\text{int}\sigma_{1}}\\
\tilde{\chi}(\xi)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

We make an arbitrarily small perturbation of the map $\tilde{\chi}^{\prime}$ on $\text{int}\sigma_{1}$ so that $\tilde{\chi}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ .

Case 2: $\sigma^{\prime}\subset\text{int}\sigma$ . Since $A\coloneqq\tilde{\chi}(\overline{\text{int}\sigma\setminus\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}})$ is a Lipschitz annulus with a common boundary and that does not cross through itself, there is a unique open set $R^{\prime}\subset U$ with $\partial R^{\prime}=A$ .

We claim that the disks $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}$ do not intersection $R^{\prime}$ . Suppose otherwise for contradiction. By the argument from Case 1, we need only suppose that $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}\sigma^{\prime})\cap R^{\prime}\neq\varnothing$ . Since $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ , we must have $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}\sigma^{\prime})\subset R^{\prime}$ in this case. Yet we observe that $\tilde{\chi}(\sigma^{\prime})$ is a nontrivial element in $H_{1}(\overline{R^{\prime}})$ , a contradiction.

We claim that $R\subset R^{\prime}$ . We consider the local picture along $\tilde{\chi}(\sigma)$ , where the 4 pieces $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ , $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ , $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ , and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ intersect with an X cross-section. We have

- • $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ are adjacent: follows from $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ .

- • $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ are adjacent: follows from the definition of $R^{\prime}$ and the fact that $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}$ do not intersect $R^{\prime}$ .

$R^{\prime}$ contains the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ contained between $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ along this intersection. Since $R$ touches $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and does not touch $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma))$ , fact (3) above implies that $R$ is the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}\tilde{D}_{i}$ contained between $\tilde{\chi}(\text{int}(\sigma))$ and $\tilde{\chi}(\text{ext}(\sigma^{\prime}))$ along this intersection. Hence, $R\subset R^{\prime}$ .

We claim that $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ . Since $\tilde{\chi}\in\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ , each component of $R^{\prime}$ touches the same side of $A$ . By the definition of $\tilde{\Omega}$ , we have either $R^{\prime}\subset\tilde{\Omega}$ or $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ . By fact (1) above, we have $R\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ , so $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}^{c}\neq\varnothing$ . Hence, $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ .

Collapse procedure: Fix a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism

$$ \psi:\overline{\text{int}\sigma}\to\overline{\text{int}\sigma^{\prime}} $$

so that $(\tilde{\chi}\circ\psi)|_{\sigma}=\tilde{\chi}|_{\sigma^{\prime}}$ . Then we define the map

$$ \tilde{\chi}^{\prime}(\xi)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\tilde{\chi}(\psi(\xi))&\xi\in\overline{\text{int}\sigma}\\
\tilde{\chi}(\xi)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$
