(1) follows directly from Theorem 5.4 and 5.7. (2) follows from Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.2 and 5.3. The proof of (3) will be given in Section 6.Finally, (4) follows from the proof of Theorem 5.7 and that $\Theta(x)=(D_{\mu}\sigma(x))^{-1}$ . The rest then follows from [12, Proposition 3.2]. ∎

## 6. Integrality of the limit varifold

We will establish in this section that the limit varifold $V$ is integral in $U$ , i.e. $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . Since $V$ is rectifiable in $U$ by Theorem 5.7, $V$ has a unique approximate tangent space $T$ at $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -a.e. $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . In other words, for any such $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ and any sequence of positive real numbers $r_{i}\to 0$ , we have

$$ (\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V\to\Theta(x)|T| $$

as varifolds 33 3 To be more precise, one can first locally isometrically embed $(\tilde{M},g)$ into some Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ and then do rescalings in $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ (c.f. [2]). Alternatively, one can also do the rescalings intrinsically using the exponential map (c.f. [35]). Both are equivalent and thus we will be using either formulation. Here, $(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V$ is the pushforward of the varifold $V$ by the map $\Phi_{r_{i}}:(\widetilde{M},g)\to(\widetilde{M},r_{i}^{-2}g)$ , $\Theta(x)$ is the $(n-1)$ -dimensional density of $V$ at $x$ and $|T|$ is the unit density varifold associated to the hyperplane $T\subset T_{x}\widetilde{M}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n}$ .

We shall assume $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ as the arguments for interior points are similar (see also [21, 38, 40] in the Euclidean setting). Fix any $r_{i}\to 0$ . We use $\tilde{g}_{i}:=r_{i}^{-2}g$ to denote the rescaled metric on $\widetilde{M}$ . Note that $(\overline{\Omega}\cap U,x,\tilde{g}_{i})\to(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+},0,g_{E})$ smoothly in the sense of pointed Cheeger-Gromov convergence. Here $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}:=\{(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;:\;x_{n}\geq 0\}$ is the upper half-space equipped with the standard Euclidean metric $g_{E}$ . Since $V_{i}\to V$ , after passing to a subsequence, we can further assume as $i\to\infty$

$$ (\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}\to\Theta(x)|T|\quad\text{ and }\quad\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}\to 0. $$

Let $\tilde{V}_{i}=(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}=\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}$ and $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}=r_{i}\lambda_{i}$ . Then $u_{i}$ satisfies, with respect to the rescaled metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ ,

$$ -\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}\Delta_{\tilde{g}_{i}}u_{i}+\frac{W^{\prime}(u_{i})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}=\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\quad\text{in $\Omega\cap U$}, $$

$$ \frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\text{on $\partial\Omega\cap U$}. $$

Note that we have $\|u_{i}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0}$ , $|\tilde{\lambda}_{i}|\leq r_{i}\Lambda_{0}\to 0$ . Moreover, by Proposition 4.15, for any fixed $R>0$ , we have for all sufficiently large $i$

$$ (E_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}(B_{R}(x),\tilde{g}_{i}))(u_{i})=\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}I_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(r_{i}R,x)\leq\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}c_{9}(E_{0}+1). $$

Therefore, all the results obtained in previous sections can be applied (with slight modifications for a convergent sequence of varying metrics). Observe that $\tilde{V}_{i}$ is the associated varifold of $u_{i}$ with respect to the rescaled metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ and $\tilde{V}_{i}\to\tilde{V}:=\Theta(x)|T|$ . Since $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\to 0$ , by Lemma 5.5, $\tilde{V}_{i}\to\tilde{V}:=\Theta(x)|T|$ is a stationary varifold with free boundary in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:=\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . As $\tilde{V}$ is supported in $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $T$ is a hyperplane, we must have $T=\{x_{n}=0\}$ .

For our convenience, by a suitable choice of coordinates, we can assume $\overline{\Omega}=\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ is equipped with a metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ converging locally smoothly to the Euclidean metric $g_{E}$ and $U=B_{4}(0)$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $4$ centered at the origin. All the balls and distances will be taken with respect to $g_{E}$ from now on. As in Section 4, we denote throughout this section $u_{i}$ , $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}$ , $\tilde{g}_{i}$ by $u$ , $\tilde{\lambda}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ , $\tilde{g}$ . We use $T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ to denote the orthogonal projection $T(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n-1})$ with respect to $g_{E}$ and $T^{\perp}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ to denote the map $T^{\perp}(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=x_{n}$ . We also define $\nu=(\nu_{1},\cdots,\nu_{n})$ to be the unit normal to the level sets of $u$ as

$$ \nu:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|}&\text{ when $|\nabla u|\neq 0$,}\\
0&\text{ when $|\nabla u|=0$.}\end{array}\right. $$

We also denote

$$ e_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}:=\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\tilde{\varepsilon}},\quad\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}:=\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}-\frac{W(u)}{\tilde{\varepsilon}}. $$

We first establish a proposition which shows that the smallness of the discrepancy and tilt excess imply the solution $u$ is close in $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ -scale to the one-dimensional heteroclinic solution near the transition region which must be rather far away from the boundary.

#### Proposition 6.1 (Sheets separation).

For any given $s,b\in(0,1)$ , there exist constants

$$ \eta_{1}=\eta_{1}(s,b,W)\in(0,1), $$

$$ L=L(s,b,W)>1 $$

such that the following holds: for any $0<\eta<\eta_{1}$ , suppose we have

- (i) $y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $T(y)=0$ and $|u(y)|\leq 1-b$ ;

- (ii) $u$ satisfies (6.2) on $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and (6.3) along $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $\tilde{\varepsilon}\in(0,1)$ , $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq\eta$ , $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y))}\leq\eta$ and $|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|\leq\eta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ on $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ ;

- (iii)

$$ \int_{B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|+(1-(\nu_{n})^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq\eta(4\tilde{\varepsilon}L)^{n-1}, $$

then $B_{3\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}=\emptyset$ , $T^{-1}(0)\cap\{x\in B_{3\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y):u(x)=u(y)\}=\{y\}$ and

$$ |I_{\tilde{\varepsilon},u}(\tilde{\varepsilon}L,y)-h_{0}|\leq s. $$

#### Proof.

Exactly the same proof (the weaker hypothesis $|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|\leq\eta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ is sufficient as pointed out in [38, Proposition 4.8]) of [21, Proposition 5.6] goes through using the up-to-the-boundary $C^{2}$ -estimates in [1] and shows that $u$ is in $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ -scale $C^{1}$ -close to the unique one-dimensional finite-energy heteroclinic solution $q(x_{n})$ satisfying $q(|y|)=u(y)$ . In particular, this implies $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{n}}\neq 0$ on $B_{3\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ from which the assertions follow by (6.3). ∎

The second proposition deals with decomposing the limit varifold $V$ into stacked single-layered interfaces. Note that by Proposition 6.1, we only need to consider the case where the transition regions stay sufficiently away from the boundary and hence the interior arguments in [21, 38, 40] go through with trivial modifications.

#### Proposition 6.2 (Stacking argument).

For any given $R,\tilde{E}_{0}>0$ , $s\in(0,1)$ , $N\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists a constant

$$ \eta_{2}=\eta_{2}(R,C_{0},\tilde{E}_{0},s,N,n,W)>0 $$

such that the following holds: for any $0<\eta<\eta_{2}$ , suppose we have

- (i) $Y\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ has no more than $N+1$ elements, $T(y)=0$ for all $y\in Y$ , diam $Y\leq\eta R$ and there exists $a>0$ such that $|y-z|>3a$ for all $y,z\in Y$ ; moreover, $U_{3a}(Y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}=\emptyset$ ;

- (ii) $u$ satisfies (6.2) on $U_{R}(Y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and (6.3) along $U_{R}(Y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}<\eta$ , $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(U_{R}(Y))}\leq\eta$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq\eta$ ; moreover, for each $y\in Y$ , we have

$$ \int_{a}^{R}\frac{d\tau}{\tau^{n}}\int_{B_{\tau}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}\xi^{+}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\leq\eta R; $$

- (iii) for each $y\in Y$ and $r\in[a,R]$ , we have

$$ \int_{B_{r}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|+(1-(\nu_{n})^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq\eta r^{n-1}, $$



$$ \int_{B_{r}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq\tilde{E}_{0}r^{n-1}; $$

then we must have

$$ \sum_{y\in Y}\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}a^{n-1}}\int_{B_{a}(y)}e_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\leq s+\frac{1+s}{\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}}\int_{U_{R}(Y)}e_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof of Proposition 6.2 requires a technical lemma similar to [21, Lemma 5.4] except that we have a weaker hypothesis on the upper bound of the discrepancy function (c.f. [38, Proposition 4.7]). We then argue exactly the same way by plugging in the radial vector field centered at a point in $Y$ which is cutoff radially and along the $x_{n}$ -direction (c.f. the proof of [21, Lemma 5.4]) and control the error terms in the monotonicity formula as in Lemma 4.12 and Proposition 4.14. ∎

The third proposition says that the energy is uniformly small in $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ outside the transition region (c.f. [21, Proposition 5.1] and [40, Proposition 4.5]).

#### Proposition 6.3 (Uniform smallness of energy outside transition region).

Suppose that $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}\leq 1$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq 1$ . Given $s>0$ , there exist positive constants

$$ \varepsilon_{12}=\varepsilon_{12}(s,C_{0},n,W)>0, $$

$$ b=b(s,C_{0},n,W,E_{0})\in(0,1) $$

such that for any $0<\tilde{\varepsilon}<\epsilon_{12}$ , we have

$$ \int_{B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u|\geq 1-b\}}\frac{W(u)}{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\leq s. $$

The proof of Proposition 6.3 requires two lemma as in [21]. Define

$$ Z_{\alpha}:=\left\{x\in B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;|u(x)|\leq\frac{1+\alpha}{2}\right\}. $$

#### Lemma 6.4.

Suppose that $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}\leq 1$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq 1$ . There exist positive constants

$$ \varepsilon_{13}=\varepsilon_{13}(W)>0, $$

$$ c_{13}=c_{13}(n,W)>0, $$

such that for any $0<\tilde{\varepsilon}<\varepsilon_{13}$ , $x\in B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $|u(x)|<1-\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\beta}$ for some $\beta$ satisfying

$$ \frac{1}{c_{13}|\log\tilde{\varepsilon}|}<\beta<\min\left\{\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{c_{13}\tilde{\varepsilon}|\log\tilde{\varepsilon}|}\right\}, $$

then we have

$$ \operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{\alpha})\leq c_{13}\beta\tilde{\varepsilon}|\log\tilde{\varepsilon}|. $$

#### Proof.

We argue exactly the same way as in [21, Lemma 5.2] except that we have to modify the function $\psi$ suitably for our problem. By a translation, we assume $x=0$ instead and denote $\tilde{\Omega}=\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}(\Omega-x)$ . By Fredholm alternative, for any $0<R<\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ , there exists a unique solution $\varphi=\varphi_{R}$ to the following mixed boundary value problem:

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\Delta\varphi=\frac{\kappa}{4}\varphi&\text{on $B_{R}(0)\cap\tilde{\Omega}$},\\
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{along $B_{R}(0)\cap\partial\tilde{\Omega}$},\\
\varphi=1&\text{along $\partial B_{R}(0)\cap\tilde{\Omega}$}.\end{array}\right. $$

Note that $\varphi_{R}$ is continuous on $\overline{B_{R}(0)\cap\tilde{\Omega}}$ up to the corner $\partial B_{R}(0)\cap\partial\tilde{\Omega}$ . Moreover, $\varphi_{R}>0$ by the strong maximum principle and unique continuation property (see e.g. [26, Section 1.8]). We can then define $\psi_{R}=(\varphi_{R}(0))^{-1}\varphi_{R}$ which satisfies

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\Delta\psi_{R}=\frac{\kappa}{4}\psi_{R}&\text{on $B_{R}(0)\cap\tilde{\Omega}$},\\
\frac{\partial\psi_{R}}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{along $B_{R}(0)\cap\partial\tilde{\Omega}$},\\
\psi_{R}(0)=1.&\end{array}\right. $$

Using Harnack inequality and Schauder estimates [1], there exists a constant $c_{13}>0$ depending only on $n$ and $\kappa$ such that $\psi_{R}(x)>e^{|x|/c_{13}}$ for all $|x|\geq 1$ . Using $\psi_{R}$ in place of $\psi$ , the rest of the proof follows from the arguments in [21, Lemma 5.2]. ∎

#### Lemma 6.5.

Suppose that $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}\leq 1$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq 1$ . There exist positive constants

$$ \varepsilon_{14}=\varepsilon_{14}(C_{0},W,n)>0, $$

$$ c_{14}=c_{14}(C_{0},W,n,E_{0})>0, $$

such that for any $0<\tilde{\varepsilon}<\varepsilon_{14}$ and $\tilde{\varepsilon}<r<r_{3}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{L}^{n}\left(\{x\in B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{\alpha})<r\}\right)\leq c_{14}r. $$

#### Proof.

The proof follows the same covering arguments from [21, Lemma 5.3] using Proposition 4.14 (with $b=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}$ ) and the arguments in the proof of Proposition 4.13. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 6.3.

It follows exactly the same proof in [21, Proposition 5.1] using Lemma 6.4 and 6.5. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3 (continued).

We now finish the proof of Theorem 3.3 by showing that $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . We use the same notations as in the beginning of this section with $x=0\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Recall that

$$ \tilde{V}_{i}:=(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}\to\Theta_{0}|T|\quad\text{ and }\quad\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}:=\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}\to 0. $$

Our goal here is to prove that $\Theta_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$ .

First of all, by Theorem 5.4 and (6.7), we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}|=\lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}(1-\nu_{n}^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}=0. $$

Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$ be the smallest positive integer such that $N>\Theta_{0}$ . Note that $\|\tilde{g}_{i}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{R}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}\to 0$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}_{i}|\to 0$ as $i\to\infty$ . Fix an arbitrary small $s>0$ , by Proposition 6.3 and (6.8), we can choose some $b>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $i$ , we have

$$ \int_{B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\geq 1-b\}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u_{i})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}\right)\leq s. $$

With these choices of $s$ and $b$ , we choose $0<\eta<\min\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ and $L>1$ as in Proposition 6.1 and 6.2 (with $R=1$ and $\tilde{E}_{0}=c_{9}(E_{0}+1)$ ). We then define as in [21] the good set $G_{i}$ consisting of all $x\in B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}$ such that

$$ \int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}|+(1-\nu_{n}^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}\leq\eta r^{n-1}\quad\textrm{for all $r\in[4\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}L,1]$.} $$

By Besicovitch covering theorem and (6.8), we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\|\tilde{V}_{i}\|(B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}\setminus G_{i})=0 $$

and

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(T(B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}\setminus G_{i}))=0. $$

On the other hand, by (6.7) and Proposition 4.14, we obtain

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\operatorname{dist}(G_{i},T)=0. $$

Now, for any $x\in B_{1}(0)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $|t|\leq 1-b$ , we let

$$ Y:=T^{-1}(x)\cap G_{i}\cap\{u_{i}=t\}\qquad\textrm{ and }\qquad a:=L\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}. $$

We would like to apply Proposition 6.2 to this $Y$ for all sufficiently large $i$ . Note that $\|\tilde{g}_{i}-g_{E}\|\to 0$ and $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\to 0$ as $i\to\infty$ . By Proposition 6.1 and (6.10), all assumptions in (i) of Proposition 6.2 are satisfied (except perhaps the cardinality of $Y$ ) for large $i$ . Noting how the constants in Section 4 scale with respect to the blow-up radii $r_{i}\to 0$ (especially Proposition 4.10 and 4.13), (ii) is also satisfied for large $i$ . Condition (iii) is essentially the definition of $G_{i}$ , together with Proposition 4.15. Note that $Y$ cannot contain more than $N-1$ elements since otherwise we will obtain by Proposition 6.1 and 6.2 that

$$ N\leq(N+1)s+(1+s)(\Theta_{0}+s) $$

which is a contradiction when $s$ is sufficiently small (depending only on $N$ ). The rest of the argument is the same as [21, Theorem 1] and we must have $\Theta_{0}=N-1\in\mathbb{N}$ . ∎
